skills.bare:
Installs and verifies system-level open-source EDA tools required for chip layout analysis and simulation.
Checks that binaries such as klayout, iverilog, yosys and gtkwave are available on PATH.
skills.expert:
Installs and verifies the core open-source EDA toolchain needed for reverse-engineering (klayout, iverilog/verilator, yosys, gtkwave, ngspice).
Runs version checks on each binary and raises an error if any required tool is missing.
Formula: for tool in required_tools: subprocess.run([tool, '--version']) → success or EnvironmentError.
Best example: confirming `klayout --version` returns a valid string before any GDS is opened.

skills.bare:
Creates an isolated Python virtual environment with all libraries needed for GDS parsing, simulation and solving.
Installs gdstk, klayout, cocotb, pyverilog, z3-solver and vcdvcd.
skills.expert:
Builds a clean, reproducible Python virtual environment containing every library required for geometry extraction, netlist handling and SAT solving.
Installs gdstk (primary GDS reader), klayout.db, cocotb, pyverilog, z3-solver and vcdvcd.
Formula: python -m venv .venv && pip install gdstk klayout z3-solver vcdvcd pyverilog.
Best example: a fresh venv that can import gdstk and successfully open warmup/04_final.gds.

skills.bare:
Clones the official Jane Street ASIC puzzle repository and checks that all required files are present.
Verifies puzzle.gds, example_inputs.vcd and the warmup/ directory exist.
skills.expert:
Clones https://github.com/janestreet/asic-puzzle-2026 and validates the presence and integrity of critical assets.
Confirms puzzle.gds, example_inputs.vcd and the entire warmup/ hierarchy are present and non-empty.
Optionally computes a SHA-256 of puzzle.gds for integrity.
Best example: after clone, `ls puzzle.gds example_inputs.vcd warmup/04_final.gds` all succeed.

skills.bare:
Parses the known warmup netlist to confirm the toolchain can correctly read gate-level Verilog.
Acts as an end-to-end smoke test before touching the real unlabeled GDS.
skills.expert:
Loads warmup/01_netlist.v (or the power-rail version) and verifies that the parser can extract module ports, cell instances and connectivity.
Serves as the first integration test of the entire reverse-engineering flow.
Formula: parse netlist → count instances of sky130_fd_sc_hd__* cells → confirm expected ports (clk, rst_n, success, etc.).
Best example: successfully reproducing the known behaviour A + B == 496 → success from the warmup netlist.

skills.bare:
Reads a binary GDSII file and enumerates all cells, layers and polygon counts.
Builds a hierarchical summary of the layout geometry.
skills.expert:
Opens a GDSII file with gdstk (or klayout.db) and extracts the full cell hierarchy, polygon counts per layer and bounding-box information.
Produces a JSON-ready structure of every cell and its geometry statistics.
Formula: for cell in lib.cells: collect (layer, datatype, polygon_count).
Best example: running on warmup/04_final.gds and obtaining the exact list of unique (layer, datatype) pairs used by the design.

skills.bare:
Maps numeric GDS layer/datatype pairs to semantic technology names (poly, active, metal1, via1, \ldots).
Creates a lookup dictionary used by all later geometry tools.
skills.expert:
Translates the numeric (layer, datatype) pairs found in the GDS into human-readable SKY130 (or custom) layer names.
Builds the dictionary {(layer, datatype): semantic_name} that every subsequent skill relies on.
Formula: LAYER_MAP = {(65,20): 'nwell', (68,16): 'poly', (70,20): 'active', (71,20): 'contact', \ldots}.
Best example: correctly mapping the metal and via layers so that connectivity tracing can distinguish Metal1 from Metal2.

skills.bare:
Partitions the die into functional regions (core logic, I/O, power grid, output generator).
Uses spatial clustering of cell bounding boxes.
skills.expert:
Clusters standard-cell instances by physical location to separate core logic from power rings, I/O pads and the special “output generator” block.
Uses simple grid-binning or DBSCAN on cell centres.
Formula: cells whose centres lie inside the central 80 % of the die → core logic; right-hand hatched region → output generator.
Best example: isolating the hatched “output generator” block shown in layout.png so it can be ignored during early reverse-engineering.

skills.bare:
Extracts every standard-cell instance from the GDS together with its master name, origin, rotation and reflection.
Produces the raw list of placed cells.
skills.expert:
Walks the GDS hierarchy and records every cell reference: master name (or geometric hash when names are stripped), absolute origin, rotation angle and x-reflection flag.
Output is a list of CellInstance records used by all later identification and netlist stages.
Formula: for ref in cell.references → {master, origin=(x,y), rotation, x_reflection}.
Best example: obtaining the complete instance list from warmup/04_final.gds that still contains readable sky130_fd_sc_hd__* names.

skills.bare:
Computes a canonical geometric hash of each unique cell master from its active-layer polygons.
Groups physically identical cells even when names have been removed.
skills.expert:
Normalises every cell’s diffusion, poly and contact polygons to the origin and produces a stable geometric hash (SHA-256 of sorted coordinates).
Identical hashes indicate the same standard-cell type regardless of placement or missing names.
Formula: hash = SHA256(sorted([(layer, round(x,3), round(y,3)) for poly in cell])).
Best example: two NAND2 cells placed at different locations produce the identical hash and are therefore grouped together.

skills.bare:
Determines the Boolean function of each unique cell by examining its transistor-level topology.
Maps PMOS/NMOS networks onto NAND, NOR, XOR, INV, etc.
skills.expert:
Analyses the series/parallel arrangement of PMOS (pull-up) and NMOS (pull-down) transistors inside a cell to deduce its logic function.
Uses diffusion-to-poly overlaps and contact connectivity.
Formula: 2 PMOS in parallel + 2 NMOS in series → NAND2; complementary networks → INV, NOR, XOR, \ldots
Best example: correctly labelling a cell whose diffusion/poly geometry matches a sky130_fd_sc_hd__nand2_1.

skills.bare:
Identifies D-type flip-flop cells by detecting the classic master-slave latch topology.
Looks for back-to-back tri-state inverters gated by clock and clock-bar.
skills.expert:
Specialised detector that recognises edge-triggered flip-flops (DFF, DFFR, DFFS) from the presence of two transmission-gate latches controlled by complementary clocks.
Formula: cells containing ≥2 transmission gates + a clock net that fans out to both halves → positive-edge DFF.
Best example: labelling sky130_fd_sc_hd__dfxtp_1 (or its unnamed geometric equivalent) as a rising-edge flip-flop with Q output.

skills.bare:
Finds all vertical electrical connections by computing geometric intersections between vias and the metal layers above/below them.
Merges nets that touch through a via.
skills.expert:
Computes polygon intersections between via shapes and the metal polygons on the adjacent layers, thereby establishing vertical electrical continuity.
Formula: net_A ∩ via_shape ∩ net_B → merge net_A and net_B into a single electrical node.
Best example: a Via1 polygon that overlaps both a Metal1 rectangle and a Metal2 rectangle is recorded as a connection between those two nets.

skills.bare:
Performs a multi-layer flood-fill to turn touching metal polygons and vias into electrical nets.
Builds a graph of gates connected by those nets.
skills.expert:
Treats all geometrically touching polygons on the same metal layer as the same net, then merges nets that share a via, producing a complete electrical connectivity graph.
Output is typically a NetworkX DiGraph (or equivalent) with gates as nodes and directed nets as edges.
Formula: flood-fill on same-layer polygons + via merges → netlist graph.
Best example: recovering the full set of wires that connect every NAND, NOR and DFF pin in the warmup design.

skills.bare:
Assigns each net endpoint to the correct pin of a standard cell by matching geometric location against known pin coordinates.
Completes the pin-accurate netlist.
skills.expert:
For every terminal of a net, finds the unique cell instance whose pin coordinate lies within a small epsilon of that terminal.
Formula: |terminal_xy − pin_xy| < ε → assign net to that pin.
Best example: a Metal1 segment ending at (5.12, 3.40) is matched to the A pin of a NAND2 instance located at the same coordinate.

skills.bare:
Identifies the primary I/O ports (clk, rst_n, enable, input, success, out[*]) from net topology and fan-out patterns.
Labels the external pins of the design.
skills.expert:
Analyses net fan-out to discover global signals: a net that drives every DFF clock pin is labelled clk; a net connected only to reset pins is labelled rst_n; undriven nets entering the core are primary inputs.
Formula: if net.fanout ⊆ {all DFF.CLK} → port = 'clk'.
Best example: correctly tagging the single net that fans out to all flip-flop clock pins as clk.

skills.bare:
Serialises the extracted gate-level graph into a syntactically valid Verilog netlist.
Writes module ports, wires and cell instantiations.
skills.expert:
Emits a clean gate-level Verilog file from the internal connectivity graph, declaring every port, wire and standard-cell instance with correct pin connections.
Formula: for each gate: emit `{cell_type} {inst} (.A(net_x), .B(net_y), .Y(net_z));`.
Best example: producing extracted_warmup.v that iverilog can compile and that matches the behaviour of the original warmup design.

skills.bare:
Removes power/ground ties, collapses pure buffer chains and merges duplicate net aliases.
Produces a minimal, simulation-ready netlist.
skills.expert:
Prunes electrically inert VDD/GND connections, substitutes buffer-only paths with direct wires, and eliminates redundant net names.
Formula: A → BUF → BUF → B collapses to the single wire A → B.
Best example: reducing a long reset-buffer chain to a single net while preserving exact functional behaviour.

skills.bare:
Compiles the recovered Verilog netlist into a fast pure-Python cycle-accurate simulator.
Provides a clock() method that evaluates combinational logic and updates flip-flops.
skills.expert:
Turns the gate-level netlist into a Python class whose clock() method performs a topological evaluation of all combinational gates and then updates every flip-flop state.
Formula: topological_sort(circuit) → evaluate gates in dependency order each cycle.
Best example: sim.clock(data_in=\ldots) returns the new values of success and all out[*] signals after one clock edge.

skills.bare:
Replays the official example_inputs.vcd through the Python simulator and measures per-signal match rate.
Validates that the extracted netlist is functionally correct.
skills.expert:
Parses example_inputs.vcd with vcdvcd, feeds every timestep into the Python gate simulator, and computes the percentage of matching signal values.
Formula: match_rate = Σ(sim[t] == vcd[t]) / total_timesteps.
Best example: obtaining ≥99 % fidelity on the warmup design, confirming that extraction introduced no functional errors.

skills.bare:
Compiles the extracted Verilog with Icarus Verilog and compares its simulation results against the reference VCD.
Provides an independent second validation.
skills.expert:
Runs the recovered netlist through the open-source iverilog simulator as a completely independent check.
Any discrepancy between iverilog and the Python simulator (or the original VCD) indicates an extraction bug.
Formula: iverilog -o sim extracted.v testbench.v && vvp sim → compare waveforms.
Best example: both simulators produce identical success and out[*] traces on the warmup, giving high confidence before moving to the real puzzle.

skills.bare:
Partitions the netlist into functional blocks (LFSR, adder, comparator, FSM, \ldots) by graph community detection or physical proximity.
Produces a block-level view of the architecture.
skills.expert:
Applies Louvain community detection (or spatial clustering) on the gate connectivity graph to discover coherent sub-modules.
Formula: nx.community.louvain_communities(G) → clusters labelled as LFSR / adder / comparator / etc.
Best example: identifying a chain of 32 DFFs with XOR feedback as a single 32-bit LFSR block.

skills.bare:
Detects linear-feedback shift-register structures and recovers the feedback polynomial from the tap positions.
Turns gate-level XOR feedback into a mathematical description.
skills.expert:
Finds DFF chains whose D inputs are driven by XORs of selected Q outputs and extracts the corresponding primitive (or non-primitive) polynomial.
Formula: DFF[i].D = XOR(DFF[j].Q, DFF[k].Q, \ldots) → polynomial xⁿ + xʲ + xᵏ + 1.
Best example: recovering the exact taps of a 16-bit Galois LFSR used inside the design.

skills.bare:
Reconstructs the complete next-state function of any finite-state machine present in the netlist.
Builds the transition table for every reachable state.
skills.expert:
Symbolically (or by exhaustive enumeration) evaluates the combinational next-state logic for every possible encoding of the state register.
Formula: for s in 0 \ldots 2ⁿ−1: next_state(s) = eval(DFF.D logic, current_state=s).
Best example: obtaining the full 256-entry transition table of an 8-bit FSM and locating the unique state that asserts success.

skills.bare:
Converts gate-level arithmetic and comparison logic into high-level algebraic form (adders, comparators, CRC, hash, \ldots).
Reveals the mathematical purpose of the circuit.
skills.expert:
Traces carry chains, XOR trees and magnitude comparators to recover the underlying arithmetic or hashing function.
Formula: ripple-carry chain of full-adders → A + B; wide XOR tree → CRC or parity.
Best example: recognising that a block computes (A + B) == 496, matching the known warmup specification.

skills.bare:
Produces a concise natural-language description of what the whole ASIC does, based on the identified sub-modules and their interconnections.
Gives the high-level “story” of the chip.
skills.expert:
Takes the JSON description of every discovered sub-module (type, width, ports) and synthesises a short English summary of the chip’s overall function.
Best example: “The design is a 32-bit LFSR-based sequence checker that asserts success when the input stream matches a hidden golden key.”

skills.bare:
Encodes the cycle-by-cycle behaviour of the circuit as Boolean constraints for a SAT/SMT solver.
Asks “which input sequence makes success = 1?”.
skills.expert:
Creates Z3 BitVec variables for every input bit on every cycle and asserts the exact transition relation of the extracted netlist, together with the goal success == True.
Formula: for each cycle t: assert circuit_transition(state_t, input_t, state_{t+1}) ∧ success.
Best example: Z3 returning a concrete 16-bit input vector that drives success high within the required number of clocks.

skills.bare:
Exhaustively tries every possible input vector (when the space is small) through the Python simulator until success is asserted.
Simple and reliable for ≤20-bit inputs.
skills.expert:
Iterates over the entire input space (or a smart subset) and simulates each candidate after a proper reset sequence.
Formula: for x in range(2ⁿ): sim.reset(); sim.clock(x); if sim.success: return x.
Best example: scanning a 16-bit space (65 536 candidates) in under two seconds and locating the unique winning vector.

skills.bare:
Mathematically inverts a known LFSR to recover the initial seed that produces a target output sequence.
Uses linear algebra over GF(2).
skills.expert:
Given the feedback polynomial and an observed output stream, solves for the unique initial state via matrix exponentiation or Gaussian elimination over GF(2).
Formula: seed = M⁻ᴺ · target_state (mod 2).
Best example: recovering the 32-bit seed that makes the LFSR emit the exact pattern required for success.

skills.bare:
Converts the winning binary input vector into the final human-readable ASCII string.
Groups bits into 8-bit characters.
skills.expert:
Takes the bit-string found by the solver and decodes it as ASCII (or another agreed encoding) by packing every 8 bits into a character.
Formula: answer = ''.join(chr(int(bits[i:i+8], 2)) for i in range(0, len(bits), 8)).
Best example: turning the 40-bit solution 01001010\ldots into the printable string that is the official answer of the puzzle.

skills.bare:
Enforces the mandatory reset protocol: assert rst_n = 0 for at least one cycle before every new input attempt.
Prevents false negatives caused by stale flip-flop state.
skills.expert:
Wraps every simulation trial with the exact reset sequence required by the design (rst_n low, then high) before applying the candidate input.
Formula: sim.clock(rst_n=0); sim.clock(rst_n=1, data=candidate); check success.
Best example: a candidate that previously failed now correctly asserts success after the proper reset toggle is inserted.
